title: Checkpoint: Reading the Planet
objective: After this level you can use maps, coordinates, directions and time zones together to describe where any place is.
summary: A place's antipode is directly opposite through Earth's center: same latitude in the other hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours apart.

cards.headline: Dig straight down from the US. You won't reach China.
cards.body: Kids have been promised China for generations. Grab a shovel (a very long one), and let's check the claim with everything from Chapter 1.

cards.headline: The point exactly opposite
cards.body: Your antipode is the spot on the far side of Earth where a straight line through the center would pop out. Finding it takes Level 3's coordinates. Keep your latitude number but switch hemispheres, so north becomes south. Then go 180° of longitude around. Start from almost anywhere in the contiguous US and you surface in the Indian Ocean. Sorry, China.

cards.fact: Most of the world's land sits opposite ocean.
cards.context: Only about 15% of land has land on its far side. That's no shock after Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. Spain is one lucky exception. Most of New Zealand's North Island lies exactly opposite it.

cards.headline: Opposite in time, too
cards.body: Your antipode is 180° of longitude away, and Earth turns 15° an hour, so it's about 12 hours off from you. When it's noon where you stand, it's midnight there. Planning to call your antipode? One of you is going to be in pajamas.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: Why every flat map distorts the round Earth, and what each kind of map chooses to keep true.
How latitude and longitude pin down any spot, and how your phone uses satellites to find its own.
Why Earth's tilt decides where the Sun can stand overhead and where a day can last all day.
How Earth's spin sets the time zones, and where the calendar date jumps from one day to the next.

options.label: The nearest point on the Equator
options.rationale: That's just straight north or south.

options.label: The point exactly opposite it, through Earth's center
The place with the same time zone
The closest point on the prime meridian
options.rationale: Longitude matters, but the antipode is the far side of Earth.

questions.explanation: Your antipode is where a straight line through Earth's center would come out on the other side.

questions.prompt: A town sits at 30° N, 60° W. Where is its antipode?

options.label: 30° N, 120° E
options.rationale: The latitude must switch to the other hemisphere.

options.label: 60° S, 30° E
options.rationale: The two numbers have been swapped.

questions.explanation: Switch 30° N to 30° S, then go 180° around: 60° W becomes 120° E.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: why is your antipode about 12 hours off from you?

options.label: It's 180° away, and Earth turns 15° an hour
It's always across the date line
options.rationale: The date line isn't what sets the 12 hours.

options.label: It's in the opposite hemisphere
options.rationale: Switching hemispheres changes latitude, not the clock.

options.label: Its time zones are twice as wide

questions.explanation: 180° divided by 15° an hour is 12 hours, so noon for you is about midnight at your antipode.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: why does most land have ocean at its antipode?

options.label: About 71% of Earth's surface is water
Continents drift away from each other
options.rationale: Drift is far too slow to explain it.

options.label: The Equator is mostly ocean
Maps exaggerate the size of oceans
options.rationale: The antipode rule doesn't depend on maps.

questions.explanation: With about 71% of the surface covered by water, the far side of most land is ocean. Only about 15% of land is opposite land.

questions.prompt: Which pair of places are antipodes of each other?

options.label: The US and China
options.rationale: That's the old myth: most of the US is opposite the Indian Ocean.

options.label: London and Tokyo
options.rationale: Both are in the Northern Hemisphere.

options.label: The North Pole and the South Pole
Spain and Australia

questions.explanation: 90° N switches to 90° S: the two poles are exactly opposite each other.
